text_blocks.snippet: Manual therapy, while generally safe, has contraindications. These can be absolute, meaning the therapy should not be performed, or relative, meaning it should be used with caution. Absolute contraindications include conditions like vertebral malignancy, spinal cord compression, or unstable fractures. Relative contraindications include osteoporosis, hypermobility, or undiagnosed pain.
snippet_highlighted_words: vertebral malignancy, spinal cord compression, or unstable fractures

list.title: Malignancy/Tumors:
list.snippet: Patients with vertebral or bone tumors, or those with a history of cancer where metastasis is suspected, should not undergo manual therapy.

list.title: Infection/Inflammation:
list.snippet: Active infections or inflammatory conditions in the area to be treated, such as osteomyelitis or cellulitis, are contraindications.

list.title: Neurological Compromise:
list.snippet: Conditions like spinal cord compression, cauda equina syndrome, or progressive neurological deficits (e.g., worsening nerve root compression) are absolute contraindications.

list.title: Unstable Fractures/Bone Disease:
list.snippet: Recent fractures, severe osteoporosis, or conditions that weaken bone structure are contraindications.

list.title: Vascular Issues:
list.snippet: Aortic aneurysms, severe coagulation deficiencies, or vertebrobasilar insufficiency are absolute contraindications.

list.title: Osteoporosis:
list.snippet: While not an absolute contraindication, manual therapy should be used with caution in patients with osteoporosis due to the increased risk of fracture.

list.title: Hypermobility/Instability:
list.snippet: Conditions like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or other hypermobility syndromes require caution, as manual therapy could further destabilize the joints.

list.title: Undiagnosed Pain:
list.snippet: If the cause of pain is unclear, manual therapy should be avoided until a diagnosis is established.

list.title: Recent Trauma:
list.snippet: Recent injuries or surgeries may require a period of healing before manual therapy can be safely applied.

list.title: Long-term Steroid Use:
list.snippet: Steroids can weaken bone and soft tissues, increasing the risk of complications.

list.title: Rheumatological Conditions:
list.snippet: Active rheumatoid arthritis or ankylosing spondylitis may require specific precautions.

list.title: Pregnancy:
list.snippet: Certain manual therapy techniques may be contraindicated during pregnancy, especially in the later stages.

list.title: Thorough Assessment:
list.snippet: A comprehensive physical examination and patient history are crucial to identify potential contraindications.

list.title: Clinical Judgment:
list.snippet: The decision to use manual therapy should be based on a thorough understanding of the patient's condition and a careful assessment of risks and benefits.

list.title: Communication:
list.snippet: Open communication with the patient about potential risks and benefits is essential.

list.title: Monitoring:
list.snippet: Patients should be monitored for any adverse reactions during and after treatment.
